full_judgment:
4. The defendants in their objection have alleged that the suit and the application for arrest of MV CHERRY ORIENT is not maintainable in the Admiralty jurisdiction of this Court. They have alleged that the cause of action of the suit relating to the allegation of damage and loss of the cargo admittedly being against the vessel MV VICEROY and not against MV CHERRY ORIENT the latter ship cannot be arrested/attached or proceeded against in an action in rem. They have denied that MV CHERRY ORIENT was owned by the defendant No. 1 or the owner of MV VICEROY; it could not be arrested because it was not concerned in the cause of action. The defendants have alleged that under the Court of Admiralty Act, 1861 in order to render the ship MY CHERRY ORIENT to be arrested or detained or to be proceeded against in an action in rem the said MV CHERRY ORIENT itself must be instrumental in giving rise to the cause of action if any, and that the alleged remedy of the plaintiff cannot be enforced against any other ship other than that in which the goods were carried to Bangladesh, and as such admiralty action in rem against vessel MY CHERRY ORIENT is not maintainable in law and the order of arrest is liable to be vacated and the Bank Guarantee furnished may be returned. 

 7. Mr Siddique Ahmed Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff has made elaborate submissions to press his contentions that under the Admiralty jurisdiction of this court a suit both in personam as well as in rem against a ship or its owner, carrier and agent of the ship or against any person who is interested and exercises control, management over the ship is maintainable and that in an action in Admiralty jurisdiction any property of the defendant or a sister ship owned by the defendant within the jurisdiction of the court can be arrested or detained. He has submitted that this court having derived its Admiralty jurisdiction from the practice and procedure of High our of Admiralty of England and the English Statutes, namely, the Admiralty Court Act, 1861, Colonial Court of Admiralty Act, 1890 and the amendments thereof as made by British Parliament, the Administration of Justice Act, 1956 or at least its principles as regards the Jurisdiction of the High Court of Admiralty of England as has been vested by the said Act can be applied while exercising jurisdiction of this Court of Admiralty. According to him even before the enactment of Administration of Justice Act, 1956 the High Court of Admiralty in England exercised jurisdiction over the properties and ships of the owner which was not connected with the cause of action. In support of his contention that a sister ship can be arrested in an action in rem or in personam, he has referred to the passage in Note Nos. 88 and 90 at pages 48 and 49 of Halsbury's Laws of England, Volume, I (Third Edition) and the observations made in AIR 1437 Calcutta 122 (123). The learned Advocate has also referred to the observations made by the Hon'ble Appellate Division of this Court in the decision reported in 34 DLR (AD) 110 (paras 9-10). According to the learned Advocate even before the Administration of Justice Act, 1956 High Court of Admiralty of England ordered arrest/detention of any property belonging to any defendant within the tidal waters of England when the defendant failed to appear or the offending ship could not be arrested. 

 9. At the outset it should be stated that this Court in exercising Admiralty Jurisdiction has derived its jurisdiction from the Admiralty Court Act, 1861, Colonial Court of Admiralty Act, 1890 and Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act (India). 1891. It is not disputed that this Court would exercise the same jurisdiction after the enactments of the said Colonial Court of Admiralty Act, (India) 1891 as the High Court of Admiralty of England exercised in 1890 under Admiralty Court Act of 1861. In England originally a suit in a Court of Admiralty and the jurisdiction of the Court was based on practice and the judgments of the Judges. But after the enactments of laws governing Admiralty jurisdiction since 1840, i.e. with the passing of Admiralty Court Act, 1840 the field of jurisdiction was defined. Thereafter with the passing of Admiralty Court Act, 1861 the Jurisdiction of the High Court of Admiralty in England appears to be based more on statute than on practice. These enactments of the statutes in England was possibly due to conflict of jurisdiction between the country Courts and the Court of Amorally. However by virtue of the provision of section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act. 1861 the jurisdiction of High Court of the England was statutorily assigned to that Court over any claim of account of damage done to the goods by negligence or misconduct or for breach of any contract on the part of the owners, master, crews, etc. of the ship. Section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861 was, however, repealed by section 21 of the Administration of Justice Act, 1920 which was again repealed by section 226 of the Supreme Court of Judicature Act, 1925. Thereafter by section 49 of the Admiralty Jurisdiction Act, 1956, section 226 of 1925 Act was repealed. It is not disputed that by section 3 of the Administration of Justice Act, 1956 the jurisdiction of the Admiralty Court in England was enlarged empowering the High Court of Admiralty of England to arrest any ship of the defendant in an action before it although that ship was not concerned in the cause of action. Before passing of the Administration of Justice Act, 1956 the Court of Admiralty in England, however, did not exercise in any action in rem by arresting of a ship of the defendant other than that which was not involved or connected in the cause of action. 

 14. Mr Siddique Ahmed Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff has submitted that though the Administration of Justice Act, 19515 is not a law of Bangladesh but since the Admiralty Court of Bangladesh has been exercising the jurisdiction on basis of English laws beginning from the Admiralty Court Act of 1861, though the provision of that Act which was the foundation of the jurisdiction of Admiralty Court of Bangladesh had been repealed and never enacted in Bangladesh and Colonial Court of Admiralty Act, 1890 of British Parliament which is not a law of Bangladesh, this Court similarly can exercise jurisdiction on the basis of the Administration of Justice Act, 1956 by arresting the ship of the defendant though it was not concerned with the cause of action. 

 In support of his contention be has referred to the decisions reported in 20 DLR 25 and 2 All ER 274 (277). I am unable to agree with the learned Advocate' "for 'the plaintiff that this court can exercise jurisdiction on the principle of the aforesaid English' Act 'of 1956 on the ground that this Court on the basis of laws of British Parliament' and the repealed section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861 had been exercising admiralty jurisdiction. The learned Advocate in this connection has referred to the observations of the Hon'ble Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh reported in 34 DLR (AD) 110 (114) wherein the Hon'ble Judges have observed thus: 

 "Thus the jurisdiction was enlarged and all that is required is that the claim must arise out of an agreement of carriage of goods, it is evident there-has been a sea change in the law since 1861. In 1861 Act the words damage done to the goods occupied a central place and the words 'breach of duty' or 'breach of contract' were related to the goods carried into any port in England or Wales but in 1956 Act jurisdiction was conferred to hear and determine any claim arising out of any agreement relating to the carriage of goods in ship". 

 16. Be that as it may, as regards the submission of the learned Advocate that the principles of the Administration of Justice Act, 1956 extending jurisdiction of the High Court of Admiralty of England can be followed by this Court, it appears to me that by virtue of Colonial Court of Admiralty Act (India) 1891, the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh has been vested with the same powers as were exercised by the High Court of Admiralty of England. The High Court Division of this Court exercises the same jurisdiction as was conferred upon the High Court of England or the High Court of Admiralty of England by virtue of the provisions of section 2(2) of the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act, 1890. The jurisdiction under section 6 of Admiralty Court Act, 1861 of this High Court Division is being exercised by virtue of the provisions of Colonial Court of Admiralty Act, 1890 and Colonial Court of Admiralty (India) Act, 1891. 

 17. It will appear that this court exercises admiralty jurisdiction by virtue of specific legislation of Imperial Parliament and the Indian Legislation Council; the High Court of Bengal or the High Court of East Pakistan or the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh has never exercised Admiralty jurisdiction on the basis of practices or the uncodified laws upon which the Court of Admiralty of England exercised its jurisdiction before the law relating to Admiralty jurisdiction of England were defined and extended by Administration of Justice Act, 1840. Following of practices and unmodified laws by the Admiralty Court in England was discontinued long before the advent of the nineteenth century. The Admiralty Court of England exercises jurisdiction on the basis of statute laws. This Court similarly exercises jurisdiction as has been given to it under section 6 of the Act of 1861 by virtue of the provision of section 2(2) of Colonial Court of Admiralty Act, 1890 and as such Administration of Justice Act, 1956 is not applicable in Bangladesh. In view of my above discussion I hold that this court exercising Admiralty jurisdiction has no power to arrest any property or ship of the defendant No. 1 than the one which was concerned in the cause of action. Thus for the consignment having been allegedly carried by MY VICEROY the arrest of MV CHERRY ORIENT cannot be maintained.
